t: Introduction — why learning how to learn is the master skill
s: What this guide is, who it is for, why most people were never taught to learn, and how to get the most out of the chapters that follow.

h.t: A note on honesty and effect sizes

p: Part I — Foundations: how learning actually works

t: What learning actually is
s: A precise definition of learning, the three stages every memory passes through (encoding, consolidation, retrieval), the different kinds of memory you possess, and why "I understood it in the lecture" is not the same as having learned it.

h.t: Kinds of memory (and why they need different training)
Understanding versus remembering versus being able to do
The forgetting curve — and why it is your friend
Putting it together: a model of learning to carry with you

p: Part I — Foundations: how learning actually works

t: The brain that learns — neuroplasticity and what actually changes
s: What physically happens in your brain when you learn — synapses, myelin, the hippocampus and neocortex — how plasticity changes across the lifespan, and what the neuroscience does and does not tell you about how to study.

h.t: Synaptic plasticity: cells that fire together wire together
Structural plasticity: the brain rebuilds itself
The hippocampus and the neocortex: two learning systems
The basal ganglia and cerebellum: the skill system
Attention, dopamine, and the gates of plasticity
Plasticity across the lifespan: is it too late?
Neuromyths: what the biology does *not* say
What the biology tells you to do

p: Part I — Foundations: how learning actually works

t: Memory systems — working memory, long-term memory, schemas and chunking
s: The functional architecture of memory — the four-item bottleneck of working memory, the near-limitless long-term store, how schemas and chunks let experts bypass the bottleneck, and what this means for organising anything you want to learn.

h.t: Why schemas are the key to learning
The dark side: schemas cause misconceptions
Chunking: how experts beat the bottleneck
Why this matters for how you learn
Forgetting: how the warehouse loses things

p: Part I — Foundations: how learning actually works

t: Cognitive load theory — managing the bottleneck
s: John Sweller's cognitive load theory explained — intrinsic, extraneous and germane load, the worked-example, split-attention, redundancy and expertise-reversal effects — and how to use it to choose materials, structure sessions and stop drowning in detail.

h.t: The effects: what the research found
Cognitive load and the "minimal guidance" debate
Applying CLT to your own learning
Reducing extraneous load in the environment

p: Part I — Foundations: how learning actually works

t: Attention, focus and the myth of multitasking
s: How attention works and why it is the true gatekeeper of learning; the real cost of task-switching and media multitasking; what the research says about phones, notifications and background media; and how to build the capacity for sustained focus.

h.t: Sustained attention: the biology of focus
Media multitasking makes you worse at attention, not better
The mere presence effect — smaller than you've been told
Blocking mobile internet: a causal test
Background music, noise and where you study
Attention and the illusion of productivity

p: Part I — Foundations: how learning actually works

t: Desirable difficulties and the illusion of fluency
s: Why the study methods that feel best usually work worst — the Bjorks' theory of desirable difficulties, the fluency illusion, why learners systematically choose badly, and how to tell productive struggle from unproductive struggle.

h.t: The paradox at the heart of learning
Judgments of learning are biased in predictable ways

p: Part I — Foundations: how learning actually works

t: Retrieval practice — the testing effect
s: The single most powerful learning technique known — what the research shows, why pulling information out of your head beats putting it back in, how to do it for facts, concepts, procedures and skills, and the mistakes that neutralise it.

h.t: Effort: make it recall, not recognition
Feedback: always, but not necessarily immediately
Success rate: aim for hard but mostly achievable
Spacing: retrieval and spacing are multiplicative
Repetition: three successful retrievals, spaced, is a good target
Format variation: retrieve in more than one way
Match the demand of the target
Retrieval practice for different kinds of knowledge
Techniques, from simplest to most structured

t: Spaced repetition — the spacing effect and how to schedule it
s: Why spreading study over time beats massing it, what the research says about optimal intervals, how spaced-repetition algorithms (Leitner, SM-2, FSRS) work, how to use Anki and similar tools without drowning in reviews, and how to space learning that doesn't fit on flashcards.

h.t: What the research says about intervals
The lag effect and the retention-interval trade-off
Building a spaced schedule for an exam

t: Interleaving and variability — mixing it up
s: Why practising A, B and C mixed together beats practising AAA then BBB then CCC, when interleaving helps most and when it doesn't, the related power of varied practice, and how to build both into study and skill training.

h.t: Discrimination: learning to tell things apart
When interleaving helps — and when it doesn't
It helps less or not at all when:
Studying from a textbook or course

t: Elaboration, self-explanation and generation
s: How to make new knowledge stick by connecting it to what you already know — elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, the generation effect, and the discipline of asking "why" and "how" — plus the evidence for each and the traps to avoid.

h.t: Connecting to what you already know
The catch: elaboration must be accurate and must be accompanied by retrieval

t: Dual coding, multimedia principles and worked examples
s: How combining words with visuals improves learning (and how it differs from "visual learning style"), Richard Mayer's evidence-based multimedia principles, how to make and use your own diagrams, and the right way to learn from worked examples.

h.t: Using dual coding as a learner
Worked examples: how to actually learn from them

t: Metacognition — knowing what you know
s: The skill of monitoring and regulating your own learning — why self-assessment is systematically biased, how to calibrate it, the planning–monitoring–evaluating cycle, and the concrete habits that turn you into your own effective teacher.

h.t: The hindsight bias in checking answers
Judge by retrieval, not by feeling
Make confidence explicit, then score it
Study your errors as a category
The regulation cycle: plan, monitor, evaluate
Metacognitive knowledge: knowing how learning works

t: What doesn't work — myths, low-utility techniques and snake oil
s: An honest audit of popular study methods and learning claims — rereading, highlighting, summarising, learning styles, brain training, speed reading, cramming, "10,000 hours", the 10% brain myth and more — with the evidence for each, and what to do instead.

h.t: Low-utility techniques that almost everyone uses
"Multitasking is a skill you can develop"
The learning pyramid ("we remember 10% of what we read, 20% of what we hear… 90% of what we teach")
"Discovery learning is best" / "Direct instruction is best"
"Attention span is now 8 seconds" (shorter than a goldfish)
How to evaluate the next claim

t: Note-taking that actually helps you learn
s: What notes are for (and what they aren't), the encoding and storage functions, handwriting versus typing without the hype, the Cornell method, outlining, sketchnotes and Zettelkasten, how to take notes from lectures versus books, and how to turn any notes into retrieval practice.

h.t: The single most important variable: generative versus verbatim
Handwriting versus typing: the actual state of the evidence

t: Reading to learn — deep reading, active reading and reading strategically
s: How to read textbooks, papers and non-fiction so that the content stays with you — previewing, questioning, reading for structure, the SQ3R family and what the evidence says about it, reading screens versus paper, how to read a scientific paper, and why speed reading is a dead end.

h.t: Reading is not learning — unless you make it so
Before you read: preview and question
While you read: read for meaning and structure
After you read: retrieve, then review
Reading like a researcher: how to read a scientific paper
Reading fiction and literature for learning
Speed reading, skimming and reading less

t: Mnemonics and memory techniques
s: The memory techniques of orators and memory champions — the method of loci, peg systems, the major system, keyword method, acronyms and stories — what the research says about how well they work, what they are good for and not good for, and how to integrate them with spaced retrieval.

h.t: What mnemonics are and why they work
The evidence: what mnemonics are good for

t: Deliberate practice and the development of expertise
s: What separates practice that builds expertise from practice that merely logs hours — Ericsson's deliberate practice, the honest state of the "10,000 hours" and talent debate, the stages of skill acquisition, plateaus and how to break them, and how to design practice for any skill.

h.t: The mechanism: building and refining mental representations
The honest state of the debate
Set a specific, measurable practice goal
The role of the teacher — and of teaching yourself

t: Transfer, analogy and mental models
s: Why knowledge so often fails to transfer beyond the situation where it was learned, what the research on near and far transfer actually shows, how analogical reasoning and abstraction can be trained, and how to build a working repertoire of mental models that apply across domains.

h.t: Transfer is mostly near and mostly hard
Transfer is possible — under specific conditions
How to actually acquire mental models

t: Problem solving, the Feynman technique and learning by teaching
s: How to get better at solving problems — Pólya's method, heuristics, focused and diffuse thinking, the Einstellung trap — and why explaining things to others (or to a rubber duck) is one of the most powerful learning acts available, with the evidence for the "protégé effect".

h.t: Problem solving as the test of understanding
The other half: learning by teaching
How to use teaching to learn

t: Feedback — getting it, using it, giving it
s: Why feedback is the most powerful and most variable influence on learning — what kinds work, when to get it, why praise and grades often backfire, how to seek and process feedback as a learner, and how to give feedback that improves someone else's learning.

h.t: The most powerful and most dangerous influence
Levels of feedback: what it points at
Giving feedback that helps others learn
The feedback loop as the unit of learning
